answer.generated: In a distributed database, deadlock occurs when transactions hold locks on some resources while waiting for others, creating a circular wait condition. Mutual exclusion ensures only one transaction at a time accesses a resource, but hold and wait means a transaction holding locks may block waiting for additional locks, leading to deadlock if no preemption is possible. To prevent deadlock, at the transaction level, pessimistic locking or time-limited locks can enforce strict ordering. At the system level, global lock managers or optimistic concurrency control can break cycles. For example, a two-phase locking protocol ensures all locks are acquired before any are released, preventing circular waits.
